chapter_title: Limiting Work In Progress (WIP) and Managing Flow
chapter_summary:
Limiting Work In Progress (WIP) is arguably the most critical practice in Kanban, directly impacting a team's ability to deliver value efficiently and effectively. The rationale behind WIP limits stems from the fundamental principle that multitasking is inefficient. When teams try to work on too many things simultaneously, they inevitably suffer from context switching, which introduces overhead as individuals frequently shift their focus between different tasks. This constant switching leads to increased errors, reduced quality, and significantly longer completion times for individual items. Imagine a chef trying to cook 20 different dishes at once versus focusing on completing a few dishes perfectly before starting the next batch. The latter approach leads to higher quality, faster delivery for each dish, and less stress.

Excessive WIP creates a multitude of negative consequences. Firstly, it obscures bottlenecks. When every column on a Kanban board is full, it's impossible to tell where the actual choke points are. Secondly, it leads to longer lead times and cycle times because work items spend more time waiting in queues rather than being actively processed. Thirdly, it increases the risk of defects, as rushed work and constant context switching make it easier to introduce errors. Fourthly, it reduces team morale and increases stress, as team members feel overwhelmed and constantly behind. Finally, it ties up capital and resources in unfinished work, delaying the realization of value. By setting explicit WIP limits for each column (or stage) on the Kanban board, you force the team to focus on completing existing work before pulling new work into that stage. For example, if your "In Development" column has a WIP limit of 3, developers cannot start a fourth task until one of the current three tasks moves to the next stage (e.g., "In Testing").

This mechanism of pulling work only when capacity becomes available is known as a **pull system**. Unlike a "push system" where work is pushed onto the next stage regardless of its capacity, a pull system ensures that work is only initiated when there's an actual demand and capacity to handle it. This creates a smoother, more predictable flow, reduces queues, and inherently highlights bottlenecks. When a column reaches its WIP limit, it signals that the downstream stage is overloaded or that the current stage needs to finish its work before taking on more. This visual cue prompts the team to swarm on blocked items or help colleagues clear the current stage, fostering collaboration and a shared responsibility for flow.

Setting WIP limits effectively is an evolutionary process. You don't necessarily start with perfect numbers. A common approach is to start with your current average WIP for each stage and then gradually reduce it, observing the impact on flow and quality. Another method is to base limits on the number of people available to work in that stage (e.g., if you have 3 developers, a WIP limit of 3 or 4 for "In Development" might be a good start). The key is to experiment and adjust. If a WIP limit is too low, it might starve downstream stages. If it's too high, it negates the benefits. The goal is to find the "sweet spot" that optimizes flow.

Managing flow involves continuously monitoring how work moves through the system and actively working to improve its predictability and speed. This requires understanding key flow metrics:
*   **Lead Time:** The total time from when a customer requests an item until it is delivered. This includes all waiting and processing time.
*   **Cycle Time:** The time from when active work begins on an item until it is completed and delivered. This is typically a subset of Lead Time.
*   **Throughput:** The number of work items completed per unit of time (e.g., tasks completed per week).

By tracking these metrics, teams can gain objective insights into their performance. For example, if Lead Time is consistently high, it suggests that items are spending too much time waiting. If Throughput is low, it indicates inefficiencies in processing. The Cumulative Flow Diagram (CFD), which we'll explore in the next chapter, is an excellent tool for visualizing these metrics.

Identifying bottlenecks is a continuous process. Visually, a bottleneck appears as a column with a large number of cards piled up, often exceeding its WIP limit, while subsequent columns are relatively empty. Once a bottleneck is identified, the team must proactively address it. Strategies include:
*   **Swarming:** The entire team (or available members) focuses their efforts on clearing the bottleneck by helping with tasks in that stage.
*   **Reducing batch size:** Breaking down large work items into smaller, more manageable pieces so they can flow through the system faster.
*   **Addressing blockers:** Immediately resolving any impediments that are preventing work items from moving forward.
*   **Cross-training:** Ensuring team members have diverse skills so they can assist in different stages when needed.
*   **Automating repetitive tasks:** Freeing up human capacity from manual work.

A common mistake is setting WIP limits but not enforcing them, or allowing exceptions to become the norm. This undermines the entire system. Another mistake is focusing solely on individual productivity rather than the flow of work for the entire team. Kanban emphasizes optimizing the *system* rather than individual utilization. By diligently applying WIP limits and actively managing flow, teams can achieve faster delivery, higher quality, and a more sustainable pace of work.

screens.subtitle: Why explicit WIP limits and active flow management speed delivery and improve quality

narration.text: In this lesson we will learn why constraining Work In Progress is the single most powerful habit a Kanban team can adopt. Limiting WIP reduces context switching, exposes hidden bottlenecks, and makes the system predictable so teams can deliver value more reliably. Think of a kitchen: a chef who focuses on three dishes at a time finishes them faster and with higher quality than a chef juggling twenty plates. That practical contrast explains the cost of multitasking and why Kanban uses explicit limits. We will also learn what a pull system is, how to choose starting WIP numbers, and which flow metrics—Lead Time, Cycle Time, and Throughput—tell you whether a change helped. The chapter closes with practical tactics for clearing bottlenecks: swarming, reducing batch size, resolving blockers, cross-training, and automation. By the end you will be able to spot a bottleneck on a real board, suggest an immediate swarming action, and propose a reasonable first WIP limit based on team size. Think about a recent project where too many open tasks slowed you down—we'll use that experience as an example to make these ideas concrete.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Limit simultaneous work to reduce context switching, reveal bottlenecks, and create a pull-driven flow that improves speed and quality.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: In this set of objectives we clarify the measurable skills you will practice. First, you'll explain why limiting WIP reduces context switching and improves quality. That means you will confidently describe the mental cost of multitasking and how WIP limits create a focus discipline. Second, you'll diagnose the consequences of excessive WIP, including longer lead and cycle times and hidden bottlenecks, with a concrete example from a Kanban board snapshot. Third, you'll describe how a pull system works: rather than pushing work forward, downstream capacity pulls work when it is ready, making flow predictable. Finally, you'll learn strategies to set and adjust WIP limits, using team size, current average WIP, and incremental experimentation. Each objective ties a concept to a practical action: explain, identify, describe, and propose changes on a real board. These are observable behaviors you can demonstrate in a review meeting or a coaching session. As you progress, look for opportunities to apply a simple WIP reduction and then measure lead time and throughput to see the effect.

Metrics to measure flow

Learn the definitions and how to use them in experiments.

Lead Time

Cycle Time

Throughput

Number of items completed per unit of time, e.g., per week.

Practical use
  • Measure cycle time before and after reducing WIP to confirm improvement.
  • Use throughput to check if delivery rate rises as WIP falls.
  • Watch lead time to ensure customer experience improves end-to-end.
Bottleneck signal

A column consistently exceeding its WIP limit while downstream columns are emptier is the clearest visual sign of a bottleneck. That observation triggers interventions like swarming or reducing batch size.

Key takeaway

Metrics let you verify whether changes to WIP limits actually speed delivery and reduce waiting.

screens.title: Why limit WIP? The rationale
screens.subtitle: Multitasking, context switching, and the chef analogy

narration.text: Limiting WIP starts with a simple claim: multitasking is inefficient. When people switch between tasks they pay a mental tax—context switching costs—because they must unload and reload the problem state, tools, and intentions. In software work that looks like toggling repositories, re-familiarizing with requirements, or rebuilding local environments. The chapter uses a chef analogy: a chef cooking many dishes at once creates a higher chance of error and longer completion times for each dish, while focusing on fewer dishes allows faster, better outcomes. A concrete example: a developer juggling five tasks will take longer to finish any one task than if they focused on two sequentially. This delays the moment the team can gather feedback from users, increasing lead time. A common misconception is thinking high individual utilization equals higher throughput; in Kanban the focus is on flow for the entire system, not individual busyness. When you limit WIP you force prioritization and completion discipline. That change often prompts cultural shifts—team members help each other more, rather than hoarding work—and makes bottlenecks visible because columns with too many cards stand out. Reflect: what ongoing switching costs do you experience now, and which small WIP change might reduce them?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: WIP limits reduce context switching and force completion, improving flow and quality.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Why limit WIP?

Multitasking costs

Context switching increases error rate and delays completion. Limiting WIP is a practical antidote.

Concrete example

A developer with five open tasks spends time re-opening branches, re-reading specs, and restoring context, lengthening cycle time for each item.

Misconception

High individual utilization is not the same as system throughput. Busy people can hide slow flow.

Analogy

A cook focusing on a few dishes completes each faster and with higher quality than a cook juggling many. The principle transfers to knowledge work.

Key Takeaway

Reducing WIP reduces context switches and shortens cycle time for individual items.

Check your understanding

Name one task you could stop starting right now to finish two tasks faster this week.

screens.title: How WIP limits create a Pull System
screens.subtitle: From push to pull — work moves when capacity exists

narration.text: A pull system is a workflow practice where downstream capacity signals when it can accept new work. Imposing a WIP limit on a column effectively creates that signal: when the column has free slots, teammates may pull the next card; when it is full, no new work is pulled until something completes. This contrasts with a push system where work is handed to the next stage regardless of readiness, which causes buildup and unpredictability. A concrete example is an 'In Testing' column with WIP limit three: testers only accept new items when fewer than three are waiting. The immediate benefits are visible: fewer queues, clearer priority of what to finish next, and an invitation to collaborate when limits are reached. A common mistake is treating a pull system as a strict blockade. Instead, it is a conversational cue—when a column fills, the team discusses why and chooses the right intervention: swarm, move blocked items to a blocked column, or adjust the limit. Over time pull systems help teams match arrival rate to processing capacity, making flow steadier. Ask yourself: what downstream stage in your workflow could most benefit from a pull signal?

keyIdea.title: Pull system
keyIdea.text: Work is pulled by capacity rather than pushed, creating predictable flow and clear signals to act.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Pull System

Creating a pull system

WIP limits act as the mechanism that enforces pull: only when capacity exists is work pulled into a stage.

Example: Testing WIP 3
Testers accept new items only when fewer than three are active, preventing an unexamined queue of waiting work.
  • Pull matches demand to capacity.
  • Full columns are a conversation starter, not simply a blockade.
  • Pull systems foster collaboration to clear space rather than piling up work.
Example scenario

When 'In Testing' hits its WIP limit, developers help write better tests or reviewers assist, so items move instead of building a queue.

Common mistake

Treating pull as a hard rule without team discussion. Use the limit as a signal to investigate, not to ignore context or urgency.

Key Takeaway

A pull system, enforced by WIP limits, creates visible demand-capacity signals that improve predictability.

screens.title: Setting and adjusting WIP limits
screens.subtitle: Start with current averages, then experiment and evolve

narration.text: Setting WIP limits is an empirical activity: you rarely pick perfect numbers the first time. Two reasonable starting heuristics are available: use the current average WIP per stage, or base limits on the number of people who can actively work in that stage. For example, if three developers usually do development work, a starting WIP of three or four for 'In Development' is sensible. Then run short experiments: reduce the limit by one, observe cycle time and throughput for a few weeks, and adjust. Watch for two failure modes. If a limit is too low it can starve downstream stages, creating idle time. If it is too high it provides no constraint and flow remains chaotic. The process looks like an iterative loop: set a hypothesis, try a change, measure lead time and throughput, and decide to keep, raise, or lower the limit. A practical rule: change only one limit at a time so you can attribute measurement changes. Also discuss exceptions in advance: an expedite lane can exist for true emergencies but it must be used sparingly and be governed by a clear policy. Ask: which column on your board would you choose to experiment with first and why?

keyIdea.title: Evolve limits
keyIdea.text: Start with averages or team size, run small experiments, measure effects, and adjust one limit at a time.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Setting WIP Limits

How to choose limits

Two pragmatic starts: current average WIP or number of people in the stage. Then iterate.

Experiment loop
  1. Set a hypothesis (e.g., reduce dev WIP by 1).
  2. Run for 2–4 weeks and measure cycle time and throughput.
  3. Decide: keep, adjust, or revert the change.
Failure modes

Too low: starves downstream work. Too high: removes constraint and hides problems.

Practical tip

Change one WIP limit at a time so you can attribute improvements to a specific action.

Key Takeaway

WIP limits should be treated as hypotheses to validate; measure and evolve them rather than setting rules and forgetting.

Check your plan

Choose one column and write a one-sentence hypothesis for a small WIP change you could try this week.

screens.title: Lead Time, Cycle Time and Throughput
screens.subtitle: Clear definitions and how to use them to judge flow

narration.text: These three flow metrics are the language of Kanban improvements. Lead Time measures the full experience from customer request to delivery, capturing waiting and processing time. Use lead time to assess customer-facing responsiveness. Cycle Time measures the duration from when active work starts until completion—it helps you evaluate internal efficiency once work has been pulled. Throughput counts completed items per time window and shows your delivery rate. A concrete scenario: if you reduce development WIP and observe that cycle time for items drops from ten days to six days and weekly throughput rises from four to six items, you have evidence your change improved flow. A common misunderstanding is to expect throughput to always rise immediately; sometimes throughput remains constant while variability drops, making delivery more predictable. Always pair metrics with visual inspections: a change that lowers cycle time but increases defects requires a different fix. The practice: record baseline metrics, run a WIP experiment, and compare median cycle time and throughput over multiple weeks before concluding success. What metric would you look at first to see whether customers will notice an improvement?

keyIdea.title: Flow metrics
keyIdea.text: Lead Time = request to delivery; Cycle Time = active work duration; Throughput = completed items per time.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Flow Metrics

Definitions you will use

Lead Time

End-to-end elapsed time from request to delivery—what customers experience.

Cycle Time

Elapsed time from when active work begins until the item is completed—internal efficiency.

Throughput

Number of items completed per chosen time interval; a measure of delivery rate.

Concrete example

Reduce dev WIP by one. Observe median cycle time drop and throughput increase over several weeks to validate improvement.

Misconception

Throughput may not rise immediately; reducing variability and lead time are often first signs of better flow.

Key Takeaway

Measure median values and compare over several weeks. Use metrics plus visual cues to judge real improvement.

screens.title: Negative consequences of excessive WIP
screens.subtitle: What goes wrong when teams try to do too much at once

narration.text: Excessive WIP produces a predictable set of problems. First, it hides bottlenecks: when every stage is full you cannot see which stage is the real choke point. Second, it increases lead time and cycle time because tasks spend more time waiting in queues. Third, defects become more likely because people rush and context switching increases cognitive load. Fourth, team morale drops as people feel overwhelmed and behind. Finally, capital and resources are tied up in unfinished work, delaying value realization. A concrete example from the chapter: a board where 'In Code Review' has four cards while its WIP limit is two. That overload indicates work piling up and blocking flow to testing and deployment. A common mistake managers make is rewarding individual utilization: high visible activity but slow delivery. The correct focus is on system flow. As you review your board, ask whether any column's stacked cards are masking a bottleneck and what immediate step—swarm, reduce batch size, or enforce the WIP—would help. Which of these negative consequences feels most familiar to your team today? Negative consequences of excessive WIP means too much wip hides bottlenecks, slows delivery, raises defects, and reduces team morale.. In practical terms, what goes wrong when teams try to do too much at once. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Consequences
keyIdea.text: Too much WIP hides bottlenecks, slows delivery, raises defects, and reduces team morale.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Consequences of Excessive WIP

Costs of too much WIP

  • Hidden bottlenecks because everything looks full.
  • Longer waiting and processing times for each item.
  • Higher defect rates due to rushed work and context switching.
  • Lower morale and tied-up resources in unfinished work.
Board snapshot example

'In Code Review' WIP limit 2, actual cards 4. That mismatch is the clearest visual sign demanding immediate action, such as swarming to complete reviews.

Pro Tip

Track lead time trends to detect growing waits before they become chronic problems.

Key Takeaway

If you see many half-finished items, the system is likely slower and riskier than it appears; reduce WIP and measure.

screens.title: Identifying and addressing bottlenecks
screens.subtitle: Swarm, reduce batch size, remove blockers, cross-train, automate

narration.text: Bottlenecks are stages where work accumulates and slows the whole system. The chapter lists concrete interventions. Swarming is when team members focus to clear the bottleneck quickly—useful when reviews or tests create temporary pileups. Reducing batch size means breaking large items into smaller pieces so they move through the system more rapidly, shortening cycle time. Address blockers immediately by making impediments visible—move blocked items to a 'Blocked' column and resolve dependencies. Cross-training builds flexible capacity so team members can help where needed, and automating repetitive tasks frees human time for value work. A concrete example: if code review is overloaded, developers can pair-review, schedule short review sessions, or create a checklist to speed reviews while maintaining quality. Beware of the trap of solving the symptom: if reviews pile up because of poor merge policies, change the policy rather than only increasing reviewer headcount. The practical habit is to inspect the board daily, discuss the top bottleneck, choose one intervention, and measure whether it reduced queue length and cycle time. What single intervention would you try first on your most common bottleneck?

keyIdea.title: Interventions
keyIdea.text: Use swarming, smaller batches, blocker visibility, cross-training, and automation to clear bottlenecks and restore flow.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Addressing Bottlenecks

Practical tactics to clear a bottleneck

Swarming

Team focuses on a set of stuck items until they flow through.

Reduce batch size

Smaller work items move faster and reveal problems sooner.

Address blockers

Make impediments visible and act immediately to resolve external dependencies.

Cross-training & automation

Build flexible capacity and free time from repetitive tasks.

Scenario

Code review pile-up: pair-review, create review standards, or schedule focused review windows to clear backlog quickly.

Key Takeaway

Pick one intervention for the top bottleneck, run it briefly, and measure whether queue length and cycle time shrink.

screens.title: Handling blocked work and visibility
screens.subtitle: Move blocked items, make impediments visible, and free capacity

narration.text: Blocked work is costly because it occupies WIP slots without progressing. The chapter recommends making blockers explicit—move blocked items to a dedicated 'Blocked' column or mark them so they do not count toward WIP if your tooling supports it. This visibility invites immediate attention: someone can take responsibility to resolve the external dependency or remove the impediment. For example, if a task is awaiting an external A P I fix, move it to Blocked and pull in another unblocked card to keep engineers productive. That action reduces idle developer time and keeps the WIP system honest. A misconception is to leave blocked cards in place and keep counting them in the WIP total; this hides capacity and prevents the team from pulling other valuable work. Use blocked markers together with short team agreements about who owns resolving different blocker types. Key habit: inspect blocked items daily, decide an owner, and track resolution time. How quickly do blocked items get ownership on your team today? Handling blocked work and visibility means make blockers visible and either move them out of counted wip or assign ownership to resolve them quickly.. In practical terms, move blocked items, make impediments visible, and free capacity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Blocked work
keyIdea.text: Make blockers visible and either move them out of counted WIP or assign ownership to resolve them quickly.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Blocked Work

Make blockers visible

Move blocked items to a visible state so they don't consume counted WIP and so someone can own their resolution.

  • Use a 'Blocked' column or a clear marker that excludes the card from WIP counts.
  • Assign ownership for blocker resolution immediately.
  • Track blocked time as a metric to identify recurring external dependencies.
Example

Card awaiting external API: move it to Blocked, assign an owner to contact the API provider, and free the development slot so another card can be pulled.

Key Takeaway

Visible blockers prevent latent WIP and enable the team to act instead of guessing capacity.

screens.title: Enforcing WIP limits — discipline versus exceptions
screens.subtitle: Why ignoring limits undermines flow and how to manage exceptions

narration.text: Setting WIP limits without enforcing them defeats the purpose. A frequent mistake is allowing exceptions to become the norm—people pull work even when a column is full because of perceived urgency or pressure. This behavior slowly erodes the discipline the limits were designed to create and preserves the same hidden queues. The correct approach is to treat the limit as a signal to investigate and agree on a response. If a true emergency appears regularly, formalize an expedite lane with clear policies rather than repeatedly violating the main limits. Another mistake is focusing on individual productivity rather than system flow. In practice, enforce a rule: when a limit is reached, discuss the cause and choose an intervention—swarm, move blocked items, or adjust the limit after measurement. If the team consistently ignores the limit, run a retrospective focused on why exceptions occur and whether underlying policies or capacity must change. The cultural point is crucial: WIP limits work when the team collectively values flow over apparent busyness. What local rule could your team adopt to treat WIP limits as a meaningful signal rather than a guideline?

keyIdea.title: Enforcement
keyIdea.text: WIP limits require consistent team agreements and measured exceptions; otherwise they lose effectiveness.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Enforcing WIP

Discipline and exceptions

Treat WIP limits as signals that trigger investigation and coordinated action. Allow exceptions only via a formal policy like an expedite lane.

Bad habit

Pulling work whenever someone is busy without discussion undermines flow.

Good practice

Treat full columns as prompts for team conversation and targeted action.

Policy example

If a true emergency arises, use an expedite lane with documented rules and a post-mortem to prevent misuse.

Key Takeaway

Consistent enforcement and clear exception policies keep WIP limits effective and trustworthy.

screens.title: Hands-on: Analyze a Kanban snapshot
screens.subtitle: Practice identifying violations and proposing immediate actions

narration.text: Let's walk through the provided Kanban snapshot to practice applying these skills. The board shows 'Ready for Dev' WIP 5 with 4 cards, 'In Development' WIP 3 with 3 cards, 'In Code Review' WIP 2 with 4 cards, 'In Testing' WIP 3 with 1 card, and 'Ready for Deployment' WIP 2 with 0 cards. Step one: identify WIP violations. Here 'In Code Review' violates its WIP limit because it has four cards but a limit of two. Step two: find the most significant bottleneck. The overloaded 'In Code Review' column is the primary choke because it blocks flow to testing and deployment. Step three: immediate action. The team should swarm on code review tasks—anyone who can review should help finish reviews or pair-review to speed decisions. Step four: handle blocked items. If Card T in development is blocked on an external A P I, move it to 'Blocked' or mark it blocked and free a development slot to pull a ready card. Finally, reflect: measure cycle time for review before and after the swarm to see whether the queue shortens and throughput increases. This is a practice you can run in a daily stand-up to make a fast, measurable improvement.

keyIdea.text: Use board snapshots to identify WIP violations, pick the highest-impact bottleneck, choose an intervention, and measure results.

screens.title: Reducing batch size to improve flow
screens.subtitle: Why smaller pieces move faster and lower risk

narration.text: Batch size strongly affects how quickly work moves through a system. Large batches take longer to finish, increase the chance of merge conflicts or integration issues, and hide problems. Reducing batch size means splitting large work into smaller, independently testable pieces that can be completed and delivered faster. A concrete example is breaking a major feature into smaller feature slices that can be tested and released incrementally. That increases throughput of small items and shortens cycle time, enabling faster feedback. However, smaller batches require more coordination and good definition of done for each slice. A common misconception is that smaller batches increase overhead; while this can be true if slices are too fine-grained, the net effect usually favors flow because items unblock sooner and defects are found earlier. A practical rule is to reduce batch size until cycle time and throughput improve, then stop. Track the trade-offs: integration effort, review overhead, and release cadence. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Reduce Batch Size

Why batch size matters

Large batches increase risk and waiting time; smaller batches deliver feedback sooner.

  • Smaller items finish faster and reduce integration pain.
  • They allow quicker testing and earlier detection of defects.
  • Slicing requires agreement on minimal, testable changes per item.
Example

Break a large feature into deliverable slices: UI, API, test harness. Each slice can be completed and validated independently.

Key Takeaway

Aim for the smallest slice that delivers value and keeps integration manageable; measure improvements in cycle time.

narration.text: This assessment checks your understanding of WIP limits in a priority conflict. The scenario: 'In Development' has a WIP limit of three and currently holds three cards. A new high-priority bug appears. The recommended action is to wait until one of the existing items moves out before pulling the new bug. That preserves system flow and prevents undermining the WIP discipline. A common alternative is to create an expedite lane for urgent work, but that lane must be governed and rare; we cannot routinely violate limits. When you encounter priority conflicts, ask: can we finish something now to free capacity, or is this truly urgent enough to use a formal expedite policy? This question is about trade-offs: immediate customer relief versus long-term system predictability. In practice, you would surface the priority in the stand-up, decide whether to swap priorities, and if necessary, use an agreed expedite channel. keyIdea.text: Respect WIP limits; wait or finish existing work before pulling new items unless a governed expedite policy exists.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Assessment

Scenario question

A WIP limit of 3 is reached. A high-priority bug appears. What should the team do?

A) Pull the bug immediately, exceeding the WIP limit.
B) Wait until one existing item moves out before pulling the bug.
C) Move an existing card to Done prematurely to make space.
D) Create an expedite lane that always ignores WIP limits.
Correct response is B: respect the limit and finish something first. An expedite lane can exist but must be rare and governed.
Key Takeaway

Prioritize finishing work to free capacity instead of routinely breaking WIP limits.

Reflect

Document any expedite uses and review them to prevent abuse and to refine your policies.

narration.text: These three concept cards capture the essentials you should remember. First, WIP limits are explicit constraints on how many items can exist in a stage at once; they create focus, reduce context switching, and expose bottlenecks. Second, a pull system means work is started only when downstream capacity exists; this reduces queues and increases predictability. Third, track Lead Time, Cycle Time, and Throughput as your primary indicators of flow health so you can measure whether a WIP change improved delivery. Keep these ideas ready when you inspect a Kanban board: ask whether WIP is excessive, which column shows the largest queue, and which metric to check to confirm an improvement. Use small experiments, observe the metrics, and iterate. That is the practical path from theory to better delivery. Work In Progress (WIP) Limits
Explicit constraints on the max items in a workflow stage that reduce multitasking and reveal bottlenecks.
Pull System
Work is pulled by available capacity downstream, preventing uncontrolled push-based queues.
Lead Time, Cycle Time, Throughput
Core metrics to measure flow and validate whether WIP changes improved delivery.
Final takeaway

Limit WIP, use pull signals, and measure flow. Experiment in small steps and validate improvements with metrics and visible board changes.

narration.text: A final quick memory aid: Work In Progress limits are a tool to reduce context switching and highlight bottlenecks; treat them as testable rules rather than rigid edicts. Bottlenecks are visible when columns exceed their WIP limits—use swarming, batching changes, or cross-training to clear them. Finally, always pair any change with measurement: track cycle time and throughput to know if your action improved flow. These three reminders help you translate daily board observations into focused experiments that yield measurable improvements.
